problems.title: Cloakroom Free Tag
problems.story: A theatre cloakroom hands out numbered tags, 1, 2, 3 and so on, and the attendant always gives the next guest the lowest-numbered tag that is not already on a hook. The tags on the hooks are read by a worn scanner that also logs zeros, negative numbers and stray large numbers, and it sometimes logs the same tag twice.
problems.statement:
You are given every number the scanner logged, in the order it read them.

A tag number is in use if it appears in the log. Zero and negative numbers are scanner noise and are never tag numbers.

Return the smallest positive whole number that is not in use. If the log is empty, that is 1.
problems.inputFormat: Every number is one value the scanner logged, in scan order. Values can be zero, negative or larger than the number of values, and the log may be empty.
problems.outputFormat: Return one integer: the smallest positive number that does not appear in the log.

parameters.name: logged
parameters.description: Every value the scanner logged, in scan order, noise included.

constraints: A solution in linear time using constant memory beyond the values exists

examples.explanation: Tags 1, 2, 3 and 7 are in use; 3 is logged twice and -5 is noise. The smallest positive number missing is 4.
Tag 1 is not on any hook, so it is the one to hand out, however many larger tags are in use.
Every tag from 1 to 5 is in use, so the next free tag is 6, one more than the number of logged values.

testCases.explanation: The worked example.
Tag 1 is free even though larger tags are in use.
An empty log: tag 1 is free.
One tag in use, and it is tag 1.
Every tag from 1 to 9000 in shuffled order: the answer is one past the length of the log.
The extreme 32-bit values and zero are noise or out of range; only tag 1 counts.
Repeated tags must not make an in-place placement loop forever, or be counted as different tags.
Every value but 1 is present, including the value one past the length of the log.
Each value sits one slot to the left of its home, so placing them in position forms one long cycle of swaps.
Nine thousand values: most tags up to 6000 with one gap, repeats, and noise.

hints: With n logged values, at most n different tags can be in use. What is the largest the answer can be?
The answer is between 1 and n + 1, so only values from 1 to n matter. If each such value v sat at position v - 1, the first position holding the wrong value would name the answer.
Swap each value into its home position until the value at the current position is out of range or its home already holds it. Every swap settles one value for good, so there are at most n swaps.

editorial.overview: With n values, at most n different tags from 1 to n can be in use, so the answer lies between 1 and n + 1. The question becomes which of 1 to n are present, and an array of n slots can record exactly that. Cyclic placement, swapping every in-range value into the slot its value names, does it in place and in linear time.
editorial.bruteForceApproach: Sort a copy and walk it, or put every value into a hash set and test 1, 2, 3 and so on until one is missing. Sorting costs O(n log n); the hash set is O(n) time but O(n) extra memory.
editorial.optimalApproach: Copy the values into a working array a (the parameter is read-only in some languages). For each position i, while a[i] is between 1 and n and a[a[i] - 1] does not already hold a[i], swap a[i] with a[a[i] - 1]. Then scan for the first position i with a[i] != i + 1 and return i + 1; if every position matches, return n + 1. Comparing against a[a[i] - 1] rather than against i + 1 is what stops a repeated value from swapping forever.
editorial.correctnessProof: A swap moves a value v into slot v - 1, and a value already in its home slot is never moved again, because the loop only moves values whose home does not hold them yet. Each swap settles one more slot, so there are at most n swaps. Afterwards, for every v from 1 to n that occurs in the log, slot v - 1 holds v: when the scan passed the position holding v, it moved v home unless home already held v. And slot i can hold i + 1 only if i + 1 occurs. So the first slot i with a[i] != i + 1 gives the smallest missing number, i + 1, and if no slot is wrong then 1 to n are all in use and the answer is n + 1.
editorial.timeComplexity: O(n): at most n swaps in total, plus a final scan.
editorial.spaceComplexity: O(n) for the working copy of a read-only input; O(1) beyond the input if it may be modified.

problems.title: Backdrop Flat Span
problems.story: A theatre's scenery dock keeps its painted flats standing upright in one row, one metre apart. To rehearse a scene, the crew stretches a backdrop between the tops of two flats. The backdrop hangs in front of the row, so the flats between the chosen two are not in the way, but it can be no taller than the shorter of the two.
problems.statement:
You are given the height of each flat in metres, in order along the row. Neighbouring flats are one metre apart.

Choosing two different flats allows a backdrop as wide as the distance between them and as tall as the shorter of the two. Its area is that width times that height.

Return the largest area any choice of two flats allows.
problems.inputFormat: Every number is the height of one flat in metres, in order along the row. There are at least two flats.
problems.outputFormat: Return one integer: the largest backdrop area, in square metres.

parameters.name: heights
parameters.description: The height of each flat in metres, in order along the row.

constraints: The answer can be larger than 2^31 - 1

examples.explanation: The flats of height 9 and 6 are three metres apart, so they allow a backdrop 3 wide and 6 tall: 18. The two end flats are wider apart but the 4 limits them to 16.
Two flats one metre apart, both 5 tall: a backdrop of 1 by 5.
The tall flat in the middle pairs only with a flat of height 1. The two ends give 2 by 1, which beats either 1 by 1.

testCases.explanation: The worked example.
Two tall flats close together beat the two short flats at the ends.
Two flats of height zero allow no backdrop at all.
Two flats: the only choice, limited by the shorter one.
Five thousand flats at the tallest height: the area needs 64 bits.
The two tallest flats stand at the two ends with short flats between them.
Equal flats: the outermost pair wins.
Heights rising steadily: the best pair is neither the widest nor the tallest, so every inward step must give up the shorter end.
Every pair includes a flat of height zero, so the answer is 0 however tall the last flat is.
Moving inward from the taller end instead of the shorter one never reaches the two tall flats, and finds only 14 instead of 50.
Five and a half thousand random heights: fifteen million pairs for a quadratic scan.

hints: Start with the two outermost flats: no pair is wider. What would a narrower pair need in order to beat them?
A narrower pair can only win by being taller. Any pair that keeps the shorter of the two end flats is narrower and no taller, so it cannot win.
Keep a pointer at each end, record the area, then move inward the pointer at the shorter flat. Each step rules out one flat for good.

editorial.overview: A pair's area is its width times its shorter height. Starting from the widest pair and narrowing one step at a time, the only move that can ever help is to give up the shorter flat, because every remaining pair that keeps it is both narrower and limited to its height. That makes the two-pointer squeeze from both ends correct, and linear.
editorial.bruteForceApproach: Try every pair: n(n - 1) / 2 areas, which is about five billion at the largest size.
editorial.optimalApproach: Set left = 0 and right = n - 1. Record (right - left) * min(heights[left], heights[right]). If heights[left] < heights[right], move left forward; otherwise move right back. Stop when the pointers meet and return the best area. Use 64-bit arithmetic: 99,999 times 10^9 does not fit in 32 bits.
editorial.correctnessProof: Suppose heights[left] <= heights[right]. Every pair (left, j) with left < j < right is narrower than right - left and no taller than heights[left], so its area is at most the area just recorded. Discarding left therefore loses no pair that could beat the best so far; the case heights[right] < heights[left] is symmetric. Every pair is either examined or ruled out while a pair at least as large is already recorded, so the largest area is found.
editorial.timeComplexity: O(n): each step moves one pointer inward.

problems.title: Busker Encore Number
problems.story: A street musician keeps a tally of how many times each song in her set was requested this season, and lists the songs from least to most requested. On her posters she prints her encore number: the largest h such that h of her songs were each requested at least h times.
problems.statement:
You are given the request count of every song, sorted from smallest to largest.

For a whole number h, call h reachable when at least h songs were each requested at least h times. h = 0 is always reachable.

Return the largest reachable h. Because the list is sorted, the answer can be found by looking at only a logarithmic number of songs.
problems.inputFormat: Every number is the request count of one song, listed from least requested to most requested. There is at least one song.
problems.outputFormat: Return one integer: the encore number.

parameters.name: requests
parameters.description: The request count of each song, in non-decreasing order.

constraints: requests is sorted in non-decreasing order

examples.explanation: Four songs (4, 7, 8 and 8 requests) were requested at least 4 times each, but only three were requested at least 5 times.
No song was requested at all, so not even h = 1 is reachable.
Both songs were requested far more than twice, but there are only two songs, so h cannot exceed 2.

testCases.explanation: The worked example.
Two songs were requested many times, but only two songs reach 2.
One song nobody requested.
One song requested once.
Five thousand songs at the largest count: the answer is limited by the number of songs.
A huge count on one song still gives only 1.
Seven songs with the same count: the answer is the count, not the number of songs.
The answer equals a count in the list and the number of songs at or above it.
Three songs have exactly three requests; an off-by-one boundary gives 2 or 4.
Every song but the first qualifies for h = 4.
Nine thousand sorted counts.

hints: In the sorted list, the songs requested at least as often as the song at position i are exactly the ones from position i to the end. How many are there?
There are n - i of them, and each has at least requests[i] requests. So h = n - i is reachable whenever requests[i] >= n - i.
As i grows, requests[i] does not fall and n - i falls, so that condition is false and then true. Binary search for the first i where it holds; the answer is n - i, or 0 if it never holds.

editorial.overview: Sorting lines the songs up so that the songs with at least h requests are always a suffix. Whether a suffix of length n - i qualifies depends only on its first element, and the test is monotone in i, so a binary search for the boundary finds the answer in O(log n).
editorial.bruteForceApproach: Try h = n, n - 1 and so on down to 0, counting the songs with at least h requests each time: O(n^2). A single backward scan brings it to O(n), which is still linear in the number of songs.
editorial.optimalApproach: Binary search for the smallest index i in [0, n] with requests[i] >= n - i, treating i = n as satisfying it. Keep lo = 0 and hi = n; while lo < hi, let mid = (lo + hi) / 2 and set hi = mid if requests[mid] >= n - mid, otherwise lo = mid + 1. Return n - lo.
editorial.correctnessProof: Let f(i) mean requests[i] >= n - i. As i increases, requests[i] does not decrease and n - i decreases, so once f holds it keeps holding, and the binary search finds the first index i* where it holds. If f(i*) holds, the n - i* songs from i* onward each have at least requests[i*] >= n - i* requests, so h = n - i* is reachable. For any larger h, the h most requested songs start at index n - h < i*, where f fails: requests[n - h] < h, so the h-th most requested song falls short and h is not reachable. Hence n - i* is the largest reachable h.
editorial.timeComplexity: O(log n) once the list is read.

problems.title: Trail Checkpoint Ramp
problems.story: A trail race is marked by checkpoints, each with a surveyed altitude. The organisers want to time one section of the course, and so that nobody can complain the timed part was downhill, it must end no lower than it starts. They want that section as long as possible, counted in checkpoints.
problems.statement:
You are given the altitude of each checkpoint, in race order.

A timed section starts at one checkpoint and ends at a later one. It is fair when the altitude at its end is at least the altitude at its start. Its length is the number of checkpoints you move forward from the start to the end.

Return the length of the longest fair section, or 0 if there is no fair section.
problems.inputFormat: Every number is the altitude of one checkpoint in metres, in race order. There is at least one checkpoint.
problems.outputFormat: Return one integer: the length of the longest fair section, or 0.

parameters.name: altitudes
parameters.description: The altitude of each checkpoint in metres, in race order.

constraints: Ending at the same altitude as the start counts as fair

examples.explanation: Starting at the checkpoint at 20 m and ending at the one at 30 m moves forward 3 checkpoints. Nothing longer is fair: the first checkpoint is higher than everything after it, and from 20 m the last checkpoint is lower.
Every checkpoint is lower than all the ones before it, so no section is fair.
Ending at the same altitude counts as fair, so the two checkpoints form a section of length 1.

testCases.explanation: The worked example.
The best start is a low checkpoint in the middle, not the first one.
One checkpoint: no section at all, so 0.
Two checkpoints from the lowest to the highest altitude.
Altitudes rising through the whole allowed range: the whole race is fair.
The extremes: the first and last checkpoints are equal and highest.
Every checkpoint at the same altitude: equal counts as fair, so the whole race.
Altitudes falling all the way, then one checkpoint as high as the start: the whole race.
The longest fair section starts at the lowest early checkpoint and ends well before the last.
Strictly falling altitudes: no fair section, and every candidate start stays on the stack.
Eleven thousand random altitudes: sixty million pairs for a quadratic scan.

hints: Some checkpoints are never worth starting from. If an earlier checkpoint is no higher than a later one, starting at the earlier one is always at least as good.
The only useful starts are checkpoints lower than every checkpoint before them. Collect them from left to right; their altitudes strictly decrease, which is a monotonic stack.
Now sweep the ends from right to left. While the start on top of the stack is no higher than the current end, that end is the farthest one it will ever get: record the length and pop it.

editorial.overview: A monotonic stack of candidate starts, each strictly lower than every checkpoint before it, combined with a right-to-left sweep over the ends, finds the longest fair section in linear time. Each candidate is popped exactly once, at the farthest end that can close it.
editorial.bruteForceApproach: For each start, scan from the right for the first end at least as high: O(n^2), five billion comparisons at the largest size.
editorial.optimalApproach: Push index i onto a stack whenever altitudes[i] is lower than the altitude at the top of the stack, or the stack is empty. Then for j from n - 1 down to 0: while the stack is not empty and altitudes[top] <= altitudes[j], record j - top and pop. Return the largest length recorded.
editorial.correctnessProof: Some optimal section starts at a stack entry: if its start s is not on the stack, an earlier entry s' < s has altitudes[s'] <= altitudes[s], and the section from s' to the same end is fair and longer. From the bottom of the stack to the top, indices increase and altitudes strictly decrease. Take an entry s and let e be the largest index with altitudes[e] >= altitudes[s] (e >= s, since s itself qualifies). When the sweep reaches e, every entry t above s has altitudes[t] < altitudes[s] <= altitudes[e], so those entries are popped and s is popped at e, recording e - s. It cannot be popped earlier, because every end after e is lower than altitudes[s]. So every entry records its longest fair section, and the maximum is the answer.
editorial.timeComplexity: O(n): every index is pushed and popped at most once.

problems.title: Relay Water Station
problems.story: A charity relay is laid out as a chain of numbered stations: from each station runners go on to exactly one next station, until the finish. Station 0 is the start. Some numbered stations are spares that are not on the course at all. The organisers want to put the water stand at the middle station of the course.
problems.statement:
You are given, for every station, the station runners go to next, or -1 if that station is the finish. Stations are numbered from 0, and the course starts at station 0. Following the next stations from station 0 always reaches the finish without visiting a station twice.

The course is the list of stations visited from station 0 to the finish, both included. If the course has an odd number of stations, return the one in the middle. If it has an even number, return the second of the two in the middle.

Stations that are not on the course may point anywhere, even at each other in a circle. Runners never visit them.
problems.inputFormat: The number at position i, counting positions from 0, is the next station after station i, or -1 if station i is the finish. There is at least one station.
problems.outputFormat: Return one integer: the number of the middle station of the course.

parameters.name: nextStation
parameters.description: For each station, the next station, or -1 at the finish.

constraints: The course from station 0 has no loop and ends at a station whose next station is -1
A solution using constant extra memory exists

examples.explanation: The course is 0, 2, 3, 1: four stations. The two middle ones are 2 and 3, and the second of them is 3.
The course is 0, 1, 2, and the middle station is 1.
Station 0 is the finish, so the course is just station 0. Stations 1 and 2 point into it but are never visited.

testCases.explanation: The worked example.
Every station is on the course, visited in an order unrelated to the numbering.
The start is also the finish.
Two stations: the second of the two middle ones is the finish.
Ten thousand stations, all on the course, in shuffled order.
Ten thousand stations but only the start is on the course.
Many spare stations share the same next station on the course.
The spare stations point at each other in one big circle, which traps any walk that does not start from station 0.
The course runs from 0 to the highest-numbered station and then down through every number: an even length, so the second middle station.
Nine and a half thousand stations, seven thousand on the course.

hints: You could walk the course once to count its stations and again to stop halfway. Can one walk do it?
Send two markers from station 0: one moves one station per step, the other two.

Keep going while the fast marker can take two more stations. When it cannot, the slow marker is at the middle; check that this stopping rule picks the second middle station when the course length is even.

editorial.overview: Slow and fast pointers. When one pointer moves twice as fast as another along a chain, the slow one is halfway along when the fast one runs out of chain, so the middle is found in one walk, with no list of the course and no count.
editorial.bruteForceApproach: Walk the course from station 0, store every station in a list, and return the element at index length / 2, rounded down. That takes O(L) time and O(L) memory for a course of L stations.
editorial.optimalApproach: Set slow = fast = 0. While fast is not -1 and nextStation[fast] is not -1, move slow to nextStation[slow] and fast to nextStation[nextStation[fast]]. Return slow.
editorial.correctnessProof: Number the course positions 0 to L - 1. After k rounds, slow is at position k and fast at position 2k. The loop continues while positions 2k and 2k + 1 both exist, that is while 2k + 1 <= L - 1, so it stops at the smallest k with 2k + 1 >= L, which is k = floor(L / 2). That is the middle position when L is odd and the second of the two middle positions when L is even. Only stations on the course are ever visited, so the spares do not matter.
editorial.timeComplexity: O(L) for a course of L stations, at most O(n).

problems.title: Cave Survey Span
problems.story: A caving club maps a cave system as chambers joined by tunnels. The map was drawn as the cavers explored: every chamber except the entrance chamber is recorded with the chamber it was first reached from, and the tunnels form no circuits. For a training expedition the club wants the longest trip between two chambers that never walks a tunnel twice.
problems.statement:
You are given, for every chamber, the chamber it was reached from, or -1 for the entrance. Chambers are numbered from 0, in no particular order. Exactly one chamber is the entrance, and following the recorded chambers from any chamber always leads to the entrance.

Each chamber and the chamber it was reached from are joined by one tunnel, which can be walked in both directions. A trip goes from one chamber to another without walking any tunnel twice, and its length is the number of tunnels it walks.

Return the length of the longest trip. A cave with one chamber has no trip longer than 0.
problems.inputFormat: The number at position i, counting positions from 0, is the chamber that chamber i was reached from, or -1 if chamber i is the entrance. There is at least one chamber.
problems.outputFormat: Return one integer: the number of tunnels on the longest trip.

parameters.name: reachedFrom
parameters.description: For each chamber, the chamber it was reached from, or -1 for the entrance.

constraints: The tunnels form a single tree, and it may be one passage 100000 chambers deep

examples.explanation: From chamber 5 the trip 5, 3, 1, 0, 2 walks four tunnels. No trip walks five.
One chamber and no tunnels.
Chamber 2 is the entrance with chambers 0 and 1 off it, and chamber 3 is off chamber 1. The trip 0, 2, 1, 3 walks three tunnels.

testCases.explanation: The worked example.
The longest trip runs through the entrance from one branch to the other.
One chamber: no tunnels, so 0.
Two chambers and one tunnel.
A single passage ten thousand chambers deep: recursion one level per chamber overflows the stack in several languages.
Ten thousand chambers all off the entrance: every trip is at most two tunnels.
A long passage ending in a chamber with six thousand dead ends: many chambers share one parent.
The longest trip lies entirely below one chamber next to the entrance and never visits the entrance.
A deep passage numbered backwards: every chamber was reached from a higher-numbered one.
Ten thousand chambers in a random, fairly deep cave.

hints: In a tree the route between two chambers is unique, and every route has one chamber closest to the entrance.
For each chamber, how far down does its deepest branch go? The longest trip whose highest chamber is c uses the two deepest branches below c.

Children must be finished before their parent. A recursive search can run out of stack on a cave 100,000 chambers deep, so list the chambers in breadth-first order from the entrance and process that list backwards.

editorial.overview: Tree diameter by dynamic programming over subtree depths. For every chamber keep how far down its deepest branch goes, and combine the two deepest branches of each chamber. Processing chambers in reverse breadth-first order replaces recursion, which matters because the cave can be a single passage.
editorial.bruteForceApproach: Run a breadth-first search from every chamber and take the largest distance found. That is O(n^2), ten billion steps at the largest size.
editorial.optimalApproach: Build the list of children of every chamber, find the entrance, and list all chambers in breadth-first order from it. Walk that list backwards. For a chamber c, consider down[child] + 1 for each child, where down is 0 for a dead end. Set down[c] to the largest of these values, and update the answer with the sum of the two largest (or the largest alone if c has one child). Return the answer.
editorial.correctnessProof: Every trip has a unique highest chamber c, the one closest to the entrance, and consists of at most two downward paths from c into different children's subtrees. Its length is therefore at most the sum of the two largest values of down[child] + 1 at c, and that sum is achieved by following the two deepest branches. In reverse breadth-first order every child comes before its parent, so each down[child] is final when c is processed. Taking the maximum over all chambers c covers every trip.
editorial.spaceComplexity: O(n) for the children lists, the order and the depths.

problems.title: Rehearsal Room Bookings
problems.story: A community music centre takes bookings for identical rehearsal rooms. Each booking holds a room from its start minute up to its end minute. A band whose booking ends at minute t is out in time for a booking that starts at minute t. The manager wants to know how many rooms the day's bookings need.
problems.statement:
You are given the day's bookings, each as a start minute and an end minute, with the start before the end.

A room holds one booking at a time. A booking that ends at minute t and another that starts at minute t can use the same room.

Return the smallest number of rooms that gives every booking a room for its whole time. A day with no bookings needs no rooms.
problems.inputFormat: The numbers come in pairs, one pair per booking: the start minute, then the end minute. The bookings are listed in the order they were made, not in order of start time. There may be no bookings.
problems.outputFormat: Return one integer: the fewest rooms needed.

parameters.name: bookings
parameters.description: Bookings as consecutive pairs: the start minute, then the end minute.

constraints: 0 <= number of bookings <= 50000, so bookings.length is even
A booking ending at minute t does not overlap one starting at minute t

examples.explanation: At minute 11 the bookings 9-12, 10-13 and 11-14 are all running; 10-11 has just ended, so its room is free for 11-14. Three rooms are needed.
The first booking ends at minute 5, exactly when the second starts, so one room serves both.
Three bookings for exactly the same time need three rooms.

testCases.explanation: The worked example.
Bookings listed out of start order, some sharing a boundary minute.
No bookings, so no rooms.
One booking of one minute.
Three thousand bookings all covering the whole allowed range.
Bookings at the extremes of the range: the last two can share a room, the first overlaps both.
Six identical bookings, then two that start exactly when they end.
Two thousand back-to-back bookings in shuffled order: treating a shared boundary minute as an overlap gives 2 instead of 1.
Four hundred nested bookings, each inside the previous one.
Several bookings start at the same minute with different ends; the room that frees earliest must be the one reused.
Three and a half thousand random bookings.

hints: Look at the bookings in order of start minute. When a booking starts, which rooms could it go into?
It can go into any room whose current booking has ended, and the room worth checking is the one that frees up earliest.

Keep the end minutes of the rooms in use in a min-heap. For each booking in start order, if the smallest end is at or before its start, take that room over; otherwise open a new room. The heap's size at the end is the answer.

editorial.overview: Interval partitioning. Sort the bookings by start and keep a min-heap of the end minutes of the rooms in use. Reusing the room that frees earliest opens a new room only when every room is busy, which happens exactly at the moment of greatest overlap.
editorial.bruteForceApproach: For each booking's start minute, count the bookings running at that minute (start <= minute < end) and take the largest count. That is O(n^2).
editorial.optimalApproach: Sort the bookings by start minute. For each booking, if the heap is not empty and its smallest end is <= the booking's start, pop it. Push the booking's end. The heap holds one entry per room, so its final size is the answer.
editorial.correctnessProof: Any set of bookings running at the same minute need different rooms, so the answer is at least the largest number running at once. The greedy opens a new room only when the smallest end in the heap is after the new booking's start. Then every room's latest booking started no later than this start and ends after it, so all of them are running at this start minute, together with the new booking. The number of rooms after opening therefore equals a number of bookings running at one minute, so the greedy never uses more rooms than the largest overlap, and it is optimal.
editorial.timeComplexity: O(n log n) for the sort and the heap operations.

problems.title: Pneumatic Tube Alarm
problems.story: An old department store still sends messages between its counters through pneumatic tubes. Each tube runs one way, and a capsule takes a fixed number of seconds to go through it. When the manager's office raises the closing alarm, every station that receives a capsule immediately sends copies down all of its outgoing tubes. The manager wants to know how long the alarm takes to reach every station.
problems.statement:
You are given the number of stations, followed by the tubes. Stations are numbered from 0, and station 0 is the manager's office. Each tube is written as three numbers: the station it starts at, the station it ends at, and the seconds a capsule takes through it. A tube can start and end at the same station, and two stations can be joined by several tubes.

The alarm starts at station 0 at time 0. A station receives the alarm at the earliest time any capsule reaches it, and from then on it sends a copy down every tube that starts there.

Return the time at which the last station receives the alarm, or -1 if some station never receives it.
problems.inputFormat: The first number is how many stations there are. The numbers after it come in threes, one triple per tube: the start station, the end station, and the travel time in seconds. There may be no tubes.
problems.outputFormat: Return one integer: the time when every station has the alarm, or -1.

parameters.name: tubes
parameters.description: Tubes as consecutive triples: start station, end station, travel time in seconds.

constraints: 0 <= tubes.length <= 60000, and tubes.length is a multiple of 3

examples.explanation: Station 2 hears at 2 seconds and passes it to station 1 by 3 seconds, sooner than the direct 5-second tube. Station 3 hears at 3 + 4 = 7, the last.
No tube leads to station 2, so it never receives the alarm.
Only the manager's office, which has the alarm from the start.

testCases.explanation: The worked example.
The four-tube route to station 4 beats the direct tube.
Only the manager's office: it has the alarm at time 0.
Two stations and no tubes: station 1 never hears the alarm.
A chain of 3,500 slowest tubes in shuffled order: the alarm needs 35 million seconds.
Ten thousand stations, only one tube: almost every station is unreachable.
Several tubes join the same pair of stations; only the fastest matters.
A direct tube with few hops is far slower than a ten-tube route: counting tubes instead of seconds is wrong.
Self-loops, and a tube that only leads into station 0: station 3 can send but never receive, so -1.
1,500 stations and 4,000 random tubes, every station reachable.

hints: Breadth-first search counts tubes, not seconds. A route through more tubes can still arrive sooner.
Settle stations in order of arrival: among the stations not yet settled, the one with the earliest known arrival cannot be reached any sooner, because every travel time is positive.

Keep a min-heap of (time, station). Skip entries for stations already settled, and try every outgoing tube of a newly settled station. The answer is the largest settled time, if every station gets settled.

editorial.overview: Single-source shortest paths with positive weights, solved by Dijkstra's algorithm with a binary heap. Each station receives the alarm along its fastest route from station 0, so the answer is the largest shortest-path time, or -1 if a station is unreachable.
editorial.bruteForceApproach: Bellman-Ford: relax every tube, stations - 1 times over. That is O(stations x tubes), up to 2 x 10^8 relaxations at the largest size.
editorial.optimalApproach: Build outgoing adjacency lists. Set time[0] = 0 and push (0, 0). Repeatedly pop the smallest entry; if it is larger than the station's recorded time, it is stale and skipped. Otherwise, for every tube (u, v, w) from the station, if time[u] + w < time[v], update time[v] and push it. Afterwards, return -1 if any station still has no time, otherwise the largest time.
editorial.correctnessProof: When a station u is popped with its recorded time t, every unsettled station has a recorded time of at least t. Any route to u leaves the settled set through some tube into an unsettled station whose time is already at least t, and every later tube adds a positive amount, so no route reaches u sooner than t: t is u's true earliest arrival. By induction every settled time is exact. Copies are sent down every tube as soon as a station receives the alarm, so each station hears it exactly at its shortest-route time, and the last one to hear it determines the answer.

problems.title: Courtyard Sentry Posts
problems.story: A palace courtyard is paved in an n by n grid of squares. For a ceremony the guard captain must post n sentries on n different squares. Sentries who can see each other along a row, a column or a diagonal start chatting, so no two may share one. Some squares hold fountains and cannot take a sentry, though a fountain does not block anyone's view. The captain wants to know how many ways there are to post the sentries.
problems.statement:
You are given the size n of the courtyard, followed by the squares that hold fountains. Rows and columns are numbered from 0 to n - 1, and each fountain is written as its row and then its column. The same fountain may be listed more than once.

An arrangement puts n sentries on n different squares without fountains so that no two sentries share a row, a column, or a diagonal in either direction.

Return the number of different arrangements. Sentries are interchangeable, so two arrangements differ only when they use different sets of squares.
problems.inputFormat: The first number is the size n of the courtyard. The numbers after it come in pairs, one pair per fountain: its row, then its column. There may be no fountains.
problems.outputFormat: Return one integer: the number of arrangements, which can be 0.

parameters.name: fountains
parameters.description: Fountain squares as consecutive pairs: row, then column.

parameters.name: size
parameters.description: The side length n of the courtyard.

constraints: Fountains do not block the view between sentries

examples.explanation: A 5 by 5 courtyard allows 10 arrangements without fountains. The fountain in the centre square rules out the 2 that use it, leaving 8.
A 6 by 6 courtyard allows 4 arrangements without fountains. The fountains at row 0, column 1 and row 5, column 4 rule out 1 of them, leaving 3.
In a 3 by 3 courtyard any two sentries in neighbouring rows must be two columns apart, and three rows cannot all manage that: there is no arrangement.

testCases.explanation: The worked example.
An 8 by 8 courtyard with three fountains.
One square and one sentry.
The only square holds a fountain.
The largest courtyard with no fountains.
The largest courtyard with a fountain on every square of one diagonal.
Two fountains, each listed many times: a repeated fountain is still one square.
A 3 by 3 courtyard cannot take three sentries at all.
A whole row of fountains: with one sentry needed in every row, there is no arrangement.
Fountains on the four corners only; they block squares but not views.
The largest courtyard with a few fountains: tens of thousands of partial arrangements.

hints: There are n sentries and n rows, and no two share a row, so every row holds exactly one sentry. Place them one row at a time.
Before placing a sentry in a row, rule out the columns and both diagonals already taken, and that row's fountain squares. Undo the choice when you come back from the next row.

Keep the taken columns, the two diagonal directions and each row's fountains as bitmasks, shifting the diagonal masks by one as you move down a row. Then the free squares of a row are a single expression.

editorial.overview: Backtracking over rows with bitmask bookkeeping. Every row holds exactly one sentry, so the search places one per row and skips any square in a taken column or diagonal or holding a fountain. Bitmasks make each step a few machine operations, and even at n = 10 without fountains the search makes only 35,539 calls.
editorial.bruteForceApproach: Try every way of giving each row a different column, n! of them (3,628,800 at n = 10), and keep those with no shared diagonal and no fountain square.
editorial.optimalApproach: Build blocked[r], the bitmask of fountain columns in row r. Search with masks cols, left and right for the columns attacked by earlier sentries straight down and along the two diagonals. In row r the free squares are ~(cols | left | right | blocked[r]) restricted to the low n bits. For each free bit b, move to row r + 1 with cols | b, (left | b) << 1 and (right | b) >> 1. Count the times row n is reached.
editorial.correctnessProof: Every arrangement has exactly one sentry per row, so it corresponds to exactly one sequence of column choices for rows 0 to n - 1. The search excludes a square in row r exactly when an earlier sentry shares its column (cols) or one of its diagonals (left and right hold, for the current row, the columns that the earlier sentries' diagonals pass through, because each shift moves a diagonal one column per row), or when it holds a fountain. So it follows every sequence of pairwise compatible, fountain-free squares, counts each arrangement once, and counts nothing else.
editorial.timeComplexity: O(n!) in the worst case, far less in practice because attacked squares are pruned early.
editorial.spaceComplexity: O(n) for the recursion and the row masks.

problems.title: Lighthouse Stair Effort
problems.story: The keeper of an old lighthouse climbs its staircase every evening to light the lamp. Some steps are worn or slippery, and she has given each one an effort score for standing on it. From the floor or from any step she climbs either one step or two at a time, and the lamp room is just above the top step.
problems.statement:
You are given the effort score of each step, from the bottom step to the top step.

The keeper starts on the floor, below the bottom step. From the floor or from a step she moves up exactly one or exactly two steps. Moving one or two steps beyond the top step takes her into the lamp room. Standing on a step costs its effort score; the floor and the lamp room cost nothing.

Return the smallest total effort of a climb from the floor to the lamp room.
problems.inputFormat: Every number is the effort score of one step, from the bottom step to the top step. There is at least one step.
problems.outputFormat: Return one integer: the smallest total effort.

parameters.name: effort
parameters.description: The effort score of each step, from the bottom step to the top step.

constraints: The answer fits in a 32-bit signed integer

examples.explanation: Standing on the steps scored 4, 2, 3 and 1 and jumping over 9, 8 and 7 costs 10. No other climb costs less.
From the floor she can move two steps onto the 15, or one step onto the 10 and then two steps into the lamp room. The 10 is cheaper.
With one step, a single move of two steps from the floor reaches the lamp room without standing on anything.

testCases.explanation: The worked example.
Two zero-effort steps are worth aiming for, but one of the two 9s between them cannot be avoided.
One step: she can go straight from the floor to the lamp room in one move of two.
Two steps at the extremes of the score range.
Thirteen thousand steps all at the highest score.
Thirteen thousand steps of zero effort.
Equal scores: the fewest steps stood on, about half of them.
Always standing on the cheaper of the next two steps walks into a 100; the best climb plans ahead.
Alternating highest and zero scores: every 1000 can be jumped over, so the answer is 0.
Fifteen thousand random scores: exponential search is hopeless here.

hints: The last step she stands on is either the top step or the one below it, because the lamp room is one or two steps above the top.
Let best[i] be the least effort needed to stand on step i. She arrived there from step i - 1 or step i - 2, or from the floor when i is 0 or 1.
best[i] = effort[i] + min(best[i - 1], best[i - 2]), counting the floor as 0. The answer is the smaller of the last two values, and only the last two are ever needed.

editorial.overview: A one-dimensional dynamic programme over the steps. The cheapest way to stand on a step extends the cheapest way to stand on one of the two places below it, so a single pass with two running values solves it.
editorial.bruteForceApproach: Enumerate every sequence of one- and two-step moves from the floor to the lamp room and add up the steps stood on. The number of sequences grows like the Fibonacci numbers: exponential in the number of steps.
editorial.optimalApproach: Keep a and b, the least effort to stand two places and one place below the current step, both 0 because the floor costs nothing. For each step, compute c = effort + min(a, b), then shift: a = b, b = c. After the top step, return min(a, b): the climb leaves either from the top step (b) or from the step below it (a). With one step, a is still the floor's 0.
editorial.correctnessProof: By induction on i, b holds the least effort to stand on step i after processing it. The move onto step i came from one place below or two places below (the floor counts as a place with effort 0), and the cheapest climb to step i is a cheapest climb to that place plus effort[i], which is exactly what the update computes. The final move into the lamp room leaves from the top step or the one below it, so the answer is the smaller of those two least efforts.
